q: A vendor's monitoring container asks you to mount `/var/run/docker.sock`. What's the security implication?
options: It's safe if the container runs as non-root
Anything that can talk to the socket controls the daemon and can start a privileged container mounting the host's `/`: effectively root on the host
It only allows reading container logs
None, the socket is read-only by default
explain: The Docker API has no fine-grained authorisation by default. Socket access equals host root. If unavoidable, use a filtering socket proxy that allows only the read-only endpoints needed, and never expose such a container to the internet.

q: Which runtime settings reduce the impact of a remote code execution bug in your Node API? (select all)
options: `--privileged` so the app can self-heal
`--security-opt no-new-privileges`
`--read-only` with a `noexec` tmpfs for `/tmp`
`--cap-drop ALL`
explain: Dropping capabilities, a read-only root filesystem and no-new-privileges all limit what an attacker can do after getting code execution. `--privileged` removes nearly all isolation.

q: You need an npm token to install private packages during `docker build`. Which approach keeps the token out of the final image and its history?
options: `COPY .npmrc` then `RUN npm ci && rm .npmrc`
`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci` with `docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=.npmrc`
`ARG NPM_TOKEN` and pass `--build-arg`
`ENV NPM_TOKEN=...` in a builder stage only
explain: Secret mounts exist only during that `RUN` and are never written to a layer. Build args are recorded in history/provenance, deleted files remain in earlier layers, and ENV ends up in the image config of that stage (and in the cache).

q: Without user namespaces, what is UID 0 inside a container from the host kernel's perspective?
options: UID 0, restricted by namespaces, dropped capabilities, seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux
UID 65534 (nobody)
The UID of the user who ran `docker run`
An unprivileged UID like 100000
explain: Without userns remapping or rootless mode, container root is host root with restrictions. If those restrictions fail, the attacker is root on the host. That's why non-root containers matter.

Creating new users inside the container
Adding new capabilities with `--cap-add`
Pulling new images
explain: It sets the kernel's `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` flag, so executing `su`, `sudo` or any setuid binary can't raise the process's privileges.

q: Trivy reports 40 HIGH/CRITICAL vulnerabilities in your image; 35 have no fixed version. What's a sensible CI policy?
options: Switch to `latest` tags to always get fixes
Ignore scanning, it's too noisy
Fail on fixable CRITICAL (and possibly HIGH) findings, report the rest, and track accepted risks with expiry dates
Fail the build on every finding
explain: Gating on unfixable findings just trains people to bypass the gate. Fix what you can (newer base, dependency bumps), triage the rest by reachability, and document exceptions (e.g. `.trivyignore`, VEX) with expiry.

q: Which statements about SBOMs, provenance and signing are correct? (select all)
options: Keyless cosign signing in CI uses the workflow's OIDC identity and a transparency log
BuildKit can attach SBOM and provenance attestations with `--sbom=true --provenance=mode=max`
You should sign the tag rather than the digest because tags are human-readable
An SBOM lists the packages inside an image so you can quickly find affected images when a new CVE appears
explain: Tags are mutable pointers; sign and deploy **digests**, which are content hashes. SBOMs answer "where is package X?", provenance records how an image was built, and keyless signing ties a signature to a CI identity.

q: Your hardened nginx container (`--cap-drop ALL --read-only`) exits with `mkdir() "/var/cache/nginx/client_temp" failed (30: Read-only file system)`. What's the right fix?
options: Run with `--privileged`
Add a tmpfs mount for `/var/cache/nginx` (and `/run` for the pid file)
Add `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN`
Remove `--read-only`
explain: Give the process exactly the writable paths it needs via tmpfs or volumes and keep the root filesystem read-only. Removing protections is the wrong direction; `SYS_ADMIN` is nearly as bad as privileged.

q: In March 2026, attackers rewrote version tags of a popular scanner's GitHub Actions to point at credential-stealing code. Which practice would have protected pipelines using those actions?
options: Running the scanner less often
Using a larger runner
Using the `@latest` or `@master` reference
Pinning third-party actions to a full commit SHA and giving jobs minimal token permissions
explain: Tags in Git (like image tags) are mutable. A commit SHA is immutable. Combine SHA pinning with least-privilege `permissions:` so a compromised step can steal less.

q: Which are true about rootless Docker and user namespaces? (select all)
options: Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon itself as an unprivileged user
Rootless mode has trade-offs such as networking performance and binding privileged ports
`userns-remap` maps container UIDs to unprivileged host UIDs while the daemon still runs as root
Rootless mode makes `--privileged` completely safe and is the default on all Linux distros
explain: Both reduce the blast radius of an escape. Rootless isn't the default for Docker Engine (Podman is rootless by default), and nothing makes `--privileged` safe.

q: Why is a distroless or hardened base image a good runtime choice for shipit?
options: It makes Node.js run faster
It includes debugging tools by default
It contains only the runtime and its libraries: fewer packages to patch, fewer CVEs, and no shell or package manager for an attacker
It automatically signs the image
explain: Minimal images reduce attack surface and noise in scans. The trade-off is debugging without a shell, solved with ephemeral debug containers (module 09).

q: `docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'` shows `name=seccomp,profile=builtin`. What does that mean?
options: Containers get Docker's default seccomp profile, which blocks dozens of dangerous syscalls unless you override it
Seccomp is only used during builds
Only privileged containers are filtered
Seccomp is disabled
explain: The default profile is applied to every container unless you pass `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (don't) or a custom profile. Many escape techniques rely on syscalls it blocks.
